Jalâloddîn Dawwânî (d. 907/1501), who converted to Shiism after a dream, was also an active commentator on the Shaykh al-Ishrâq. To this prolific writer we owe above all a commentary on the Book of the Temples of Light, to which Ghiyâthoddîn Mansûr Shîrâzî (949/1542) replied with a counter-commentary. Two figures from Tabrîz must also be mentioned. Wadûd Tabrîzî wrote a systematic commentary on the Book of Tablets Dedicated to ’Imâdoddîn, the Seljuk emir of Anatolia.

Earlier in this study we drew upon the pages of that work dealing with the Xvarnah. The commentary was completed in 930/1524. A certain Najmoddîn Mahmûd Tabrîzî, a contemporary of Wadûd, wrote glosses on the Book of Eastern Theosophy. Let us repeat that none of these commentaries should be neglected. They correspond to the studies we publish today in specialized scholarly journals.

This somewhat dry enumeration brings us to the moment when the teaching and spiritual experience of the Shaykh al-Ishrâq reveal themselves as a true center of intellectual life, a meeting place for spiritual worlds that communicate with one another on the plane of gnosis. The Book of Elucidations (Talwîhât) had already been translated into Hebrew.

Now, in the sixteenth century, Sohrawardî's work was to spread its influence into India, while in Iran it contributed to the philosophical revival of the Safavid period. It exercised a profound influence on the circle of thinkers gathered around Emperor Akbar (1556–1605), the Mughal ruler of India, and on his generous project of an ecumenical religion (dîn-e ilâhî, religio divina). Ishrâqî theosophy was one of the sources of this search for a universal religious understanding.

At the time, a vigorous exchange of spiritual ideas developed between Iran and India, with philosophers and Sufis traveling frequently back and forth. Here we shall concentrate on two examples of the fruit borne by Sohrawardî's work in Persian, which was then the language of culture in northwestern India. One belongs to the movement that arose around Shâh Akbar's initiative. The other consists of an entire body of Zoroastrian ishrâqî literature that emerged during the same period, under the influence of the same spiritual milieu.

As we have seen, the Shaykh al-Ishraq, Suhrawardi, wrote some of his works in Persian; in a few cases he even translated his own writings from Arabic into Persian. His great trilogy, however, and The Book of Oriental Theosophy, for which the trilogy serves as a preparation, were written in Arabic. So were the major commentaries mentioned above, which helped bring his thought into the wider intellectual life of Islam.

The first example of the passage of his work into Persian that concerns us here is Mohammad Sharif ibn Harawi, who produced an extensive Persian treatment of the prologue and second part of The Book of Oriental Theosophy. It was fitting that he should concentrate on the five books making up that second part, for it is there that the Illuminationist (ishrâqî) teaching is principally set out. Nor did he confine himself to Suhrawardi's text. He translated much of Qotb Shirazi's commentary into Persian and added reflections of his own .

We know little else about the translator himself. He completed his work in 1008 AH/1600 CE, which makes him a contemporary of Mir Damad (d. 1040 AH/1630 CE), the great teacher around whom the school we have called the School of Isfahan would take shape. Mohammad Sharif's prologue also suggests that he knew Indian Sufism firsthand and had actually spent time in India. His undertaking may therefore be connected with the religious questions raised by Shah Akbar's reforms.

Our second example comes from a body of Parsi Illuminationist writing produced by Zoroastrians who had emigrated from Iran to India. About forty years ago, the Parsi scholar Dr. J. J. Modi published an important study of Azar Kayvan, a Zoroastrian high priest who moved with his disciples from Shiraz, or its surroundings, to India around the turn of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries . Suhrawardi's writings found devoted admirers among them, so the history of this group is especially revealing for the Shaykh al-Ishraq's later influence in the East.

Earlier, we saw in the outcome of Suhrawardi's great project something like a homecoming of the Hellenized Magi to Iran—though now to an Islamic Iran. With Azar Kayvan's circle, that homecoming extends into a Zoroastrian community, and the circle is complete. This also helps us understand the books written within or around the group. The Parsis of India have called them “semi-Parsi” books, but regarded them favorably enough to undertake their publication.

Let us be clear from the outset: these works have relatively little to offer a specialist in Avestan and Pahlavi philology. For a student of religious philosophy, however, they are immensely interesting. They show Suhrawardi's work being reinterpreted through what these Zoroastrians knew of the Avesta and the Pahlavi texts. How far do their readings of Suhrawardi agree with Zoroastrian belief in its full, traditional form? That is why we recalled the description “semi-Parsi.” Dr. J. J. Modi was exceptionally well placed to judge.

What is certain is that these books contain genuinely Zoroastrian material. Not all the rest can be called Suhrawardian—they also contain substantial Manichaean, Buddhist, and Sufi elements—but a reader familiar with the Shaykh al-Ishraq will still feel on familiar ground on almost every page. Their extraordinary value lies in showing us how, in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, a group of Zoroastrian mystics received the work of a thinker who had expressly set out to “revive the theosophy of the ancient Persians.”

Only a few works seem to have survived from what was apparently a fairly extensive literature, and their rarity makes them hard to obtain. One of the works belonging to this larger body of writing is the Dabestan al-Madhahib—roughly, “The School of Religious Sciences”—a rich source of information about religious life in India at that time . Its author, Mobed-Shah, maintained close contact with Azar Kayvan's disciples. It is hardly surprising, then, that he devoted considerable attention to the different branches of Zoroastrianism existing in his day; indeed, on this point he is our only source.

In Chapter XI, on the religion of the philosophers, he divides them into two great families: the Illuminationists (Ishrâqîyûn) and the Peripatetics, followers of the Aristotelian tradition. He observes, for reasons that should now be clear, that the teachings and practices of the Illuminationists correspond exactly to those he had described in his first chapter under the heading “the ancient religion of the Iranians” . There, too, we are told that this ancient Iranian sacred wisdom was also the wisdom of the ancient Greeks, up to and including Plato—just as we read in Suhrawardi and his commentators.

The chief work cited as an authority by the author of the Dabestan probably originated within Azar Kayvan's school or its immediate circle. It is called the Dasatir-Nameh, the “Collection of Sacred Books” attributed to the ancient prophets of Iran. In the past, the few Orientalists who examined it generally confined themselves to negative criticism because it did not provide the kind of text they were looking for as philologists. Certainly, anyone hoping to find a surviving fragment of the Avesta or of Pahlavi literature will be disappointed.

But we should ask the book to give us what it actually sets out to give: the reflections of Zoroastrians who, in the spirit of the Shaykh al-Ishraq, pondered a body of traditions that have yet to receive a systematic study. The work presents itself as a “Bible of the prophets of Iran,” consisting of sixteen books attributed to sixteen prophets. It is written in two languages.

Whether one of them is an invented jargon or simply a cipher matters little to us, since it comes with a clear and readable Parsi Persian “translation.” Whether that translation was really written by Sasan V, said to have lived in Iran in the time of Khosrow Parviz and frequently mentioned in this literature, is quite another matter. Historically, “improbable” would be far too mild a word.

Yet the book's contents remain fascinating for anyone tracing the history of Ishraq. The “Book of Mah Abad” and the “Book of Sasan I,” for example, offer a close reflection of Suhrawardi's metaphysics, sometimes expanded with ideas drawn from the theosophy of Iranian Sufism .

Much the same can be said of another important work from Azar Kayvan's school. Among the members of the Zoroastrian high priest's community whom the author of the Dabestan knew personally, one figure stands out: Farzaneh Bahram ibn Farshad, known as “Bahram the Younger” (Kuchak Bahram). Mobed-Shah met him at Lahore in 1048 AH/1638 CE. He tells us that Bahram had completed the full course of philosophical and theological studies; that he knew Persian, Arabic, and Hindi, as well as at least one Western language; and that he translated Suhrawardi's works into Persian .

Unfortunately, no manuscript of these translations has yet come to light. One substantial work by Farzaneh Bahram, however, Sharestan-e chahar chaman (“The City of Four Gardens”), was published by lithography in Bombay in 1279 AH/1862 CE through the efforts of four Zoroastrian mobeds, or priests. This Persian work proceeds along lines similar to the Dasatir-Nameh and has four parts.

The first three deal with the creation of the cosmos and then with the sacred history of the prophet-kings of ancient Iran, from Hushang to the last Sasanian ruler. The fourth, or “fourth garden,” deals with astronomy, the structure of the cosmos, and geography . A long account of Illuminationist theosophy follows the chapter on Zoroaster. This is not an unthinking anachronism: for this Zoroastrian Illuminationist, the chapter on Zoroaster provides precisely the right occasion to state his position toward the Islamic schools and religious groups of his own time.

One more work from the same school deserves mention: Ayin-e Hushang (“The Religion of Hushang,” Iran's primordial prophet). It was published by lithography in Bombay in 1296 AH/1879 CE by the Parsi scholar Mirza Bahram Rostam Nasrabadi, who supplied a lengthy preface. It is a substantial collection of four Persian treatises , whose manuscripts came from the imperial library. Even a quick reading reveals the influence of Ishraq.

We can do no more here than draw attention to these little-known books. This Zoroastrian Illuminationist literature calls for a study of its own, which we hope to undertake elsewhere. The author of the Dabestan also mentions other Zoroastrian sages from Shiraz whom he knew personally. Among them were Hakim Ilahi Herbad and Hakim Mirza, both described as Ishrâqîyûn. Both knew the Shaykh al-Ishraq's works thoroughly, and had absorbed his teaching so completely that they made his “Book of Hours”—from which we translated two psalms above, in Chapter III, Section 5—the liturgical ritual of their own religious life .

The understanding held by these Zoroastrian Illuminationists in Shah Akbar's time—of philosophy's Iranian origin in its two forms, ecstatic (ishrâqî) and dialectical (Peripatetic), and of the translators who disseminated learning preserved in the treasuries of the ancient Persian kings—ought to be compared with the older traditions preserved in authentic Pahlavi literature. Nor was Suhrawardi's image of the Iranian sage as a Platonist something he invented.

The historian Mas'udi (d. 346 AH/957 CE), discussing Tansar, the chaplain of Ardashir who restored the Mazdean religious establishment in the Sasanian Empire in the third century CE, already describes that eminent figure as a Platonist—or, in the terms of our texts, an Illuminationist. Tansar's own words, in his famous letter, explaining and justifying his way of life were not chosen at random. They correspond exactly to the stages that would later structure Suhrawardi's spiritual discipline .

Through the distinguished spiritual figures he met in India, the author of the Dabestan ultimately leads us back to Iran. He tells us that he learned directly from Farzaneh Bahram that among those close to Azar Kayvan's circle, and those granted meetings with the master, was none other than Baha'oddin 'Amili, one of the most eminent figures of Iranian Shiism: the venerable mujtahid, or jurist qualified to exercise independent judgment, who taught Molla Sadra in Isfahan .

Thus we find ourselves once more on Iranian soil, following the traces of the “community of the Book of Oriental Theosophy.” We have just seen this mystical community send out branches into India. Although distinct from Sufism, its history is nonetheless intertwined with Sufism's—perhaps most directly with the Nurbakhshiyya order. A distant great-grandnephew of the Shaykh al-Ishraq is said to have succeeded Sayyed Mohammad Nurbakhsh (d. 1464) as head of that order .

As for Shiism, we have already noted more than one point of contact between Illuminationist and Imamite theosophy—indeed, something far more substantial than mere points of contact. Their interaction becomes clearer still, as we recalled earlier, when Shiite theosophers recover what they recognize as their own spiritual inheritance within the theosophy of Ibn 'Arabi. The merging of these currents would mark Iran's great intellectual and spiritual flowering under the Safavids, while in India the effects of Shah Akbar's reforms were being felt at the same time, with many Iranian thinkers taking part.

The first name that comes to mind is Mir Damad (d. 1040 AH/1630 CE), the intellectual master of the School of Isfahan, whose influence is still felt in Iran today. Without examining here how far each of his writings agrees with Suhrawardi's positions, let us note a few telling details. In answering a correspondent's question about a difficult passage in Suhrawardi's Book of Oriental Theosophy, Mir Damad shows a profound understanding of the text . As for the “Profession of Faith of the Philosophers,” we have elsewhere mentioned a manuscript copied in Mir Damad's own hand, ending with the highest praise for the Shaykh al-Ishraq .

Finally, Mir Damad adopted the very name Ishraq as his pen name (takhallos). Readers who turn to the “Ecstatic Confessions” translated later in this work (Book V, Chapter I) will be able to appreciate the affinity between these two shaykhs. We may also recall that one of Mir Damad's pupils, Qotboddin Ashkevari, discerned in the Twelfth Imam the features of the figure whom Zoroastrian teachings about the end of time call the “Saoshyant,” the restorer who will raise the dead.

The full brilliance and range of Suhrawardi's thought become especially apparent, of course, in the work of Mir Damad's most celebrated pupil, Molla Sadra Shirazi. Molla Sadra left an immense body of writing, running to several folio volumes. An entire book would be needed to establish the place of the Shaykh al-Ishraq's writings and ideas within it. Here we shall mention only the Glosses Molla Sadra wrote on The Book of Oriental Theosophy: a work of remarkable depth, scale, and originality in its own right, without which much of Suhrawardi's book would lose its resonance.

We shall give a sample of these glosses later, after attempting to explain Molla Sadra's importance to the spiritual culture of Iran (below, Book V, Chapter II). Molla Sadra frequently uses the words mashriq (“east”) and mashriqî (“eastern”), and it is a pleasure to see his commentators—from Mirza Ahmad Ardakani Shirazi and Molla Isma'il Isfahani to Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i—carefully distinguish their meanings; their analyses invariably lead back to Suhrawardi's use of the words .

Later (Book V, Chapter III), we shall also devote several pages to another outstanding master, Qazi Sa'id Qommi. His work is of the greatest philosophical interest because it shows how the Shiite understanding of the Imam intersects with a fundamental Illuminationist idea.

Even after naming two eminent masters such as Molla Hadi Sabzavari and Molla 'Abdollah Zonuzzi, who carried the philosophy of Ishraq into nineteenth-century Iran, we would still have to trace its presence in the writings of another forty or fifty thinkers who have sustained philosophical life in Iran over the past four centuries. Unfortunately, the work of examining those writings—which first requires reliable editions of the texts—has scarcely begun.

This title for our final section seems to bring together, better than any other, the teachings and intentions of the Shaykh al-Ishraq. It also prepares the way for Book III, which will deal with Ruzbehan and the “Faithful in Love.”

The theme draws together connections we have suggested, sometimes only in passing: the “story” of the gnostic; the earthly self and its heavenly counterpart; the Hermetic figure of Perfect Nature and the Mazdean or Manichaean vision of the angel Daena; the idea of Sophia in Jacob Boehme; the philosophers' Active Intelligence and the Madonna Intelligenza of the Fedeli d'amore; the emergence of the mystical epic; and more. What especially concerns us is how the austere metaphysical theme of the Active Intelligence unfolds, through imagination, into a mystical epic of love.
We can see this again in one of Suhrawardi's tales of initiation.

We must say a little about it in closing, because its dramatic setting contains, in suggestive form, everything we have tried to analyze here. It resonates with so many centuries of Iranian mystical poetry that, if we attempted to set Suhrawardi's themes alongside all their later variations, the task would have no end.

Here we shall concern ourselves only with the metaphysical foundation of the religion and mysticism of love as presented in this last tale. In doing so, we shall briefly return to all the themes we have encountered throughout this book and the questions they have raised.

Our section's title is not accidental. It is inspired by a work of the Russian philosopher Boris Vycheslavtsev, who remains little known for want of translations: his Ethics of Transfigured Eros, a book of the first importance for anyone investigating the role of imagination in spiritual life . Vycheslavtsev seeks to ground moral life in the proposition that “images of the imagination possess a power of transfiguration.” His inquiry is part of a broader effort to understand transcensus: the absolute reality of transcendence, which makes it “impossible to remain within the limits of pure immanentism” and can be fulfilled only “in the sphere of the beyond, of metaphysical being.”

Accepting the findings of depth psychology, he holds that imagination alone provides the key to the subconscious because it “raises psychic energy to a higher level.” Sublimation, on this account, corresponds to the spiritual transformation of the human being, to the divinization spoken of in Christian mysticism. By recognizing sublimation as a driving force of the soul, Vycheslavtsev can propose a new ethics, one that moves beyond moralism: “The true ethics of grace is that which is capable of transfiguring and sublimating” .

Clearly, this takes us far beyond the pious but ineffective distinction between eros and agape on which so many moral theologians have insisted. We are, rather, in the current of Russian Orthodox theosophical thought that, beginning with Vladimir Soloviev, sought to recover the sacred meaning of Eros. There is also this decisive point: once imagination is granted the power to transfigure, we find ourselves on ground familiar to Ibn 'Arabi . An ethics of transfiguration and divinization corresponds to the idea of ta'alloh, well known in the philosophy of Ishraq.

We shall see that the transformation of human Eros into divine Eros is also the very heart of Ruzbehan Baqli of Shiraz's ethics (Book III, below). As for the metaphysical source of an Eros that must undergo this transformation if it is to become what it truly is, Suhrawardi attempted to suggest it in the short mystical romance to which we shall turn in closing. For us, this tale seems to express the final idea toward which the preceding discussion has been moving.

At the same time, Suhrawardi's religion of transfigured Eros, drawing on the full resources of metaphysical Imagination, brings us back to the need to recognize the distinct reality and mode of being of the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world. Only in that world can the metaphysical ground of an Eros that is both transfigured and transfiguring be inwardly “seen.” Such seeing brings to life figures who are real in their own way; it is indispensable, for without it everything would remain a merely theoretical possibility. This, ultimately, is the point where Suhrawardi's metaphysics of essences meets the dramatic world of his mystical tales.
We can indicate this connection only briefly; a full treatment would demand another book.

Yet it belongs here, because the structure of Suhrawardi's mystical romance Mu'nis al-'ushshaq makes the connection unavoidable. Its title might best be rendered Companion for the Faithful in Love . Unlike the two tales translated earlier (Chapters V and VI), this one is told in the third person rather than the first. Its dramatis personae, or figures in the drama, are the very kind that conventional literary criticism, knowing nothing of the reality of the mundus imaginalis, dismisses as “personified abstractions” or “allegories.”

We must challenge that confusion and the impoverishment of meaning it brings. Our starting point should be Avicenna's understanding of essence. An essence, considered in itself, is simply what it is, absolutely and without qualification. It is neither the logical universal of a concept nor an individual existing in the world of the senses. The logical universal requires a negative condition: we exclude from the abstract concept of an essence everything that would prevent it from being predicated of any number of individuals.

The sensory individual requires a positive condition: we determine what must be added to the essence for it to be realized in singularibus, in particular beings of the empirical world. Essence, however, is not a logical universal but a metaphysical universal. It is a spiritual form, and there is therefore no reason why an individual being cannot have an essence of its own.

We may speak, for example, of the Socrates-ness of Socrates. That is neither a logical universal that other people could share nor the physical individual Socrates encountered in the sensory world. Socrates-ness is not one of the logical universals; it is the spiritual form of an individual being. Here the principle of individuation is form, not matter, as in Aristotelian Thomism.
Thus Socrates-ness is not abstract in the sense of a logical concept; rather, it is separate (khôristos, Arabic mojarrad) from what is concrete to the senses.

But it is a mistake to reserve the word “concrete” for the sensory world. There is also a concrete reality of spirit, and this is concrete in the highest degree. That is the metaphysical position underlying Suhrawardi's teaching about angels.

An absolute essence of this kind—neither a logical universal nor a sensory individual, but possessing its own unity, its own distinctive mode of individuation, and its own specific “concrete” character—is what the Shaykh al-Ishraq calls an Angel: the lord of a species (rabb al-nû'), which bears that angel's name. Each species, together with its individual members, is the “theurgy,” the creative manifestation, of its Angel.

This brings us back to the questions raised above about the sense in which each angelic being, as lord of a species, may be called universal (Chapter III, Section 3, pp. 117–118; and Chapter VI, Section 4, p. 316).

We are now confronted with a question. If such an essence stands beyond both the logical universal and the sensory individual, how does it exist? And once we have defined its mode of existence, in what form can it appear to us concretely? Can we know it as anything other than a universal concept abstracted by the intellect? If we limit ourselves to concepts, we remain trapped in the familiar dispute about universals. If the essence is merely a pure possibility, it has no actual being.

But if it truly exists—and otherwise how could we speak of what it is?—we must decisively reject any dividing line between being and existing that would reserve existence for individual things in the sensory world.

We must acknowledge a whole scale of real modes of existence above what people commonly call “reality” today. This includes, to begin with, mental existence (wojûd dhihnî), understood as existence in the full sense of the word. That is why Molla Sadra's metaphysics of existence may ultimately be seen as preserving, rather than destroying, the metaphysics of essence.

In what concrete spiritual form, then, can an essence reveal itself to us—an essence that Suhrawardi understands as an angelic being, individualized not by some alien material element but by its own nature, which makes it one essence rather than another? Neither as a concept nor as a thing of the senses. Its place of appearance, the “stage” on which it becomes visible (mazhar), can only be the mundus imaginalis: the world in which an Angel appears either in dreams or in contemplation while awake.

There it takes the form of the figures who animate Suhrawardi's Companion, and who recur throughout the Persian mystical epic: Intelligence, Beauty, Love, and Sorrow. They can also bear familiar personal names: Adam, Joseph, Zolaykha. In every case these are proper names. Their actions, the distinctive ways they act, show that they are more than logical concepts; and the scene of those actions is not the sensory world. To explain them as “personified abstractions” explains nothing. Once an abstraction is personified, it is no longer an abstraction. An abstract person is no person at all.

Moreover, what sort of being is involved in the making (facere) or coming-to-be (fieri) of a personification? The tragedy of a culture begins when it can understand every essence only as the logical universal of a concept. Giordano Bruno, by contrast, declares: Intelligere est phantasmata speculari—to understand is to contemplate images, to think through them. We might put the difference this way: with logical universals, one writes a treatise of theoretical philosophy. With concrete individuals, one writes history or an ordinary novel.

But with metaphysical universals—with pure essences appearing at the level of concrete reality proper to them, in the mundus imaginalis—one writes a mystical epic, a visionary narrative, a tale of initiation.

This is true whether the figures in such “romances” have ordinary personal names or names that seem, at first sight, to designate concepts. They are not concepts but real beings of the mundus imaginalis. The point applies equally to The Ring of the Nibelung, to the Grail cycle to which we have repeatedly referred, to the visions of The Shepherd of Hermas, to The Romance of the Rose, to The Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreutz, and to many other writings of this kind.

All of them deserve to be read afresh as narratives of initiation—with eyes that Western philosophy and civilization have long since closed, but that our “Eastern” theosophers have kept open to the mundus imaginalis.
We can now understand, too, why merely calling such works “allegories” settles nothing.

Let us take one further example: the figures who inhabit Ramon Llull's exquisite and sublime Tree of the Philosophy of Love . In its prologue, Llull tells us how he went into “a beautiful forest, not far from Paris, thickly wooded and full of springs.” In the middle of a lovely meadow he found a great Tree; beneath its shade sat a lady of extraordinary beauty, richly dressed.

When he greeted her, she revealed her name: “Philosophy of Love.” As the author unfolds his plan, we learn that the book will introduce a number of “ladies of love”—the roots of the Tree, such as Goodness and Greatness, eighteen in all—and also “young men of love.” The latter bear names such as making-good and making-great: in each case they represent the action, the energeia, proceeding from the essence named by the noun.

Each “lady of love” is thus an essence that appears to the author in its own fully “objective” reality. It is not defined by placing it within a broader class and specifying what distinguishes it, for that would reduce the essence to its logical concept. We are dealing neither with logical concepts nor with persons inhabiting the sensory world.

Each essence makes itself known through what it brings into being: it “makes essential” what it itself is. We might express this in German as es west sein Wesen. Goodness is that through which the good makes good; Greatness, that through which the great makes great, and so on.

In short, to give expression to an essence we must add to the noun naming it something drawn from the verb facere, “to make” or “to bring about.” This active dimension—energeia, in the Greek sense—is revealed to Llull's inward sight as a “young man of love.” That is why, throughout the book, the “young men of love” speak, act, and behave as real, concrete persons. Their concrete reality belongs precisely to the mundus imaginalis; without that world, we would mistakenly reduce the entire “story” to an allegory, which it is not.

Here we should recall the Amahraspands, the archangels of Zoroastrianism (Chapter III, Section 3), because their names also express the actions they perform. They are the “Holy Immortals,” but theirs is a holiness that acts upon and transforms what it touches: a sacred, effective energy—the spanta of each Amahraspand. This energy communicates being and the growth of being by bringing into existence what it itself embodies as an essence. The Amahraspands are neither conceptual abstractions nor mere “aspects” of the supreme Godhead . They are at once distinct spiritual beings and active powers.

Suhrawardi took such pains to express this by turning his metaphysics of essences into a teaching about angels. In Llull, the relation between the spiritual being and its active power, between what the noun names and what the word for action names, is the relation between the “ladies of love” and the “young men of love.” An essence becomes visible in a person who wholly embodies and gives form to what that essence is.

Neither a logical concept nor an ordinary individual in the sensory world can perform that role. If essences did not appear as “ladies of love” and “young men of love,” as the figures do in Suhrawardi's Companion, we would have before us only their logical concepts, not the essences themselves. This is why we must recall our earlier discussion (Chapter IV, Section 4, pp. 197 ff.) of the moment when a doctrine or theory becomes the narration of an event—the A, B, and C levels of interpretation.

If Llull uses the word metaphor, we must not misunderstand the direction in which it moves. Trans-sumptio means transposition, a carrying across. When a melody is transposed into a higher key, its accuracy or “truth” does not consist in returning it to its former pitch; it consists in preserving the structure, the isomorphism, between the two versions. We have used that comparison before (Book I, Chapter IV, Section 2).

In the same way, the true meaning of concrete figures in the mundus imaginalis is not discovered by bringing them back down to the level of a logical concept. The reverse is true. The real meaning of the logical concept becomes apparent only at the level where the essence can reveal itself: in the image that is its mazhar, its stage or form of appearance, and that can be perceived by metaphysical Imagination. This is why we cited the Russian philosopher's account linking transcensus, the movement beyond the merely given, with the transfiguring power of images.

What is ultimately at issue, then, is a kind of space belonging to the spiritual world, outside the locations of the senses. Within this space, imagination can “see” the spiritual world in the setting proper to its manifestation, its mazhar. The Arabic-Persian word means a form or place of manifestation, and in ordinary use can also mean a theatre. This space corresponds to the distinctive time of the hikâyat, the first-person visionary tale.

We have repeatedly seen how such a tale escapes the dilemma that otherwise leaves us asking whether an event is myth or history. It is the space opened up by the tale's own time. Inner vision itself bears witness to what it sees, as the surah of the Star says: “The heart did not deny what it saw” (Qur'an 53:11).

We must therefore say something about the connections between the 'âlam al-mithâl, the mundus imaginalis, and some fascinating recent research, even though we must once again limit ourselves to a few preliminary observations.

I am thinking of Frances A. Yates's fine book The Art of Memory. The texts she examines seem to offer inexhaustible possibilities for our subject, especially because our “Eastern” theosophers have, understandably, been absent from the comparisons made so far.

The ancient ars memorativa, the art of memory, originally worked through two elements: places and images (loci et imagines) . Its method was to move mentally—or even bodily—through a building, such as a palace, church, or abbey with its outbuildings, placing striking images at successive locations. By revisiting those images in the mind, a speaker could follow the thread of a speech without faltering. This already implies that certain arrangements in space can reveal what lies hidden in the depths of the human mind.

Yet we must be precise about what is contemplated. Whatever building or landscape frames the exercise, the image itself is never a material one: it has never been physically placed there. The act is not external sensory perception but inner imaginative perception. The contents of memory are themselves inward spiritual forms, of which memory is the treasury; memory is the treasury of Imagination.

For that very reason, and because of the assumptions on which it rests, the ars memorativa was bound to develop between the Middle Ages and the Renaissance into a metaphysics of memory, inseparable from a metaphysics of the image and of Imagination. Such a metaphysics requires, whether openly acknowledged or not, an account of the distinctive reality of the mundus imaginalis.

Among those who developed this metaphysics of memory, we find several assumptions drawn from Hermeticism and Neoplatonism. The first, in one form or another, is that the soul existed before earthly life and fell from a heavenly, angelic state into a world of darkness and demonic oppression—as in Suhrawardi's tales. The fundamental act of self-knowledge is therefore an awakening: a recollection of what the gnostic was before entering this world.

Think here of the “Hymn of the Pearl” and the “Tale of Exile.” Such an awakening presupposes a power of memory that reaches incomparably further back than psychology ordinarily allows. It also presupposes that the Image bringing about this awakening cannot be explained by the commonplace theory that, because human beings are weak, they must clothe realities too exalted for their intellect in sensory appearances. We need instead an idea like the association of Imago and Magia found in Jacob Boehme.

In this sense the ars memorativa ultimately belongs to the ars hieratica, the sacred or theurgic art of the Neoplatonists discussed above (Chapter II, Section 1). Since the human being as microcosm reflects the macrocosm, memory becomes the memory of the “theurgic sage,” the divine human being who participates intimately in the divine powers and energies of the cosmos. Images thereby acquire, by that very fact, a theurgic and “transfiguring” power. We have already learned that, for Suhrawardi, each species is the theurgy, the “talisman,” of its Angel.

The same idea recurs among the Renaissance Hermeticists. It is embodied in the extraordinary Theatrum mundi, or Theatre of the World, constructed by Giulio Camillo and so illuminatingly explained by Yates. Reproducing the architecture of a classical theatre in miniature, according to Vitruvius's proportions, Camillo's theatre—his mazhar, as we might call it—unifies the contents of memory by grounding that unity in images drawn from the heavenly world. Its arrangement reverses the usual position of the audience and the spectacle.

The “performance” occupies the auditorium: images are placed in seven tiers of seats, arranged in seven “columns,” the seven pillars of the house of Wisdom. The observer, standing mentally on the stage (frons scenae), can take in at a glance, through contemplation of those images, the contents of all the worlds. This is something far more significant than what we ordinarily call a memory technique. As Yates writes, “the secret or one of the secrets of this theatre is that these planetary images are supposed to be talismans or to have a talismanic virtue” .

These talismanic images are, of course, inward images: they reproduce the heavenly world within the inner world of imagination and make imagination receptive to celestial influences. We find this in Marsilio Ficino as well as in Giordano Bruno. For Bruno, the images of the starry world are the Umbrae idearum, the “shadows of ideas,” closer to true reality than the physical shadows of the lower world. In a particular and limited sense, they correspond to the 'âlam al-mithâl. This is also how Bruno interprets Ramon Llull's Ars, or Art.

The ars memorativa is thus transformed into a mystery cult within the soul; there are inward images, even inward statues. We might say that the art of memory finds its completion in an ars interiorativa, an art of inward realization. Philosophy stands here at a crossroads. Wherever the full power of images and Imagination to disclose knowledge goes unrecognized, and is replaced by the logical and mnemonic arrangement of concepts, an inner iconoclasm is already close at hand, preceding the destruction of images in the outer world.

Indeed, the first iconoclasts opposed to the Renaissance Hermeticists and Neoplatonists were the Logicians, humanist or otherwise, who were so hostile to images that they would acknowledge no art of memory beyond the logical ordering of concepts. Where, by contrast, a metaphysics of the mundus imaginalis is available, spiritual realism directs us toward a concrete spiritual reality, toward the “transfigurations” brought about by the imagines agentes, the active images.

The expression imagines agentes is significant in itself because it parallels Intelligentia agens, the Active Intelligence. Just as the Active Intelligence brings the human intellect into act, so the Imago agens, the active Image, awakens and brings the imaginative faculty into act.

The imagines agentes are not “products” manufactured by imagination. They are forms of manifestation, and imagination is the place where they appear, their theatre—their mazhar. This theatre also reveals both the differences in style and the affinities between a particular form of inner imagination and a particular style of architecture. That architecture may be the architecture of the cosmos, as in the two Suhrawardian tales translated earlier. It may be something more limited, like the classical theatre of Vitruvius mentioned a moment ago. Or it may be a city or fortress, as it is on two occasions in Suhrawardi.

Indeed, everything suggests that Suhrawardi imagined, on the scale of the human microcosm, something corresponding to the idea of the Theatrum mundi: the “fortress of the soul,” whose successive floors or towers provide locations for mental images endowed with powers of memory and spiritual transformation. This fortress, described in the “Epistle of the High Towers” (above, Chapter VI, Section 6), reappears in the Companion we are about to discuss.

We needed to mention this way of giving space to spiritual realities, derived from the ars memorativa, if only to suggest the comparative studies still needed before the Shaykh al-Ishraq's work can be heard in its full resonance. Much remains to be done to understand and situate the mundus imaginalis, the theatre of his tales where these “transfigurations” take place—beginning with the transfiguration of Eros, as the brief account that follows will show.

The Companion for the Faithful in Love is chiefly concerned with a triad of these figures, commonly called “personified abstractions,” though in fact they are something quite different. Their origin takes us back once more to Avicenna's metaphysics. Neither the way they appear nor the way they act allows us to regard them as conceptual abstractions, and still less as individual people belonging to the sensory world.

Yet each has a distinct metaphysical individuality. Each is the concrete manifestation of a pure essence, appearing at the only level compatible with its nature: the mundus imaginalis. The short treatise opens by recalling a familiar prophetic tradition (hadith), already encountered in this book: “The first thing God created was the Intelligence.” This is the Nous of Greek philosophy, a distinct spiritual reality.

Philosophers in Islam found in this saying of the Prophet an invitation to Neoplatonic reflection. We have already recalled how, in Avicenna's account of the cosmos, the First Intelligence—whom Suhrawardi calls Bahman, the first of the Zoroastrian archangels—performs three acts of contemplation.

First it contemplates its own Source; second, its existence as made necessary by that Source, which constitutes its dimension of light; and third, its own essence, which, apart from its Source, would remain non-being, and so constitutes its dimension of shadow. From these three contemplations proceed, respectively, a Second Intelligence, the First Soul (Anima mundi, the Soul of the World), and the first heaven.

The Soul longs in love to be united with the Intelligence from which it proceeds. The heaven, composed of the subtlest matter and arising from the dimension of shadow, marks the ideal distance separating the Intelligence from the Soul. It is the Soul's loving longing for its Intelligence that sets this heaven in motion. Already, in this cosmic drama of the archangels, we have the first transfiguration of Eros on the scale of the universe.

At precisely this point, the Companion brings the drama into the world of human experience. The three beings arising from the Intelligence's contemplation now appear as three persons. They no longer bear their original names in the creation of the cosmos—Intelligence, Soul, and Heaven—but names expressing how they appear within the human soul, at the level where the religion of transfigured Eros comes into being. Their names are Beauty, Love, and Sorrow, respectively.

The three members of this triad thus correspond to Intelligence, Soul, and the Soul's Heaven. Their names are no longer common nouns but proper names, designating three pure essences. They are neither logical universals nor individuals of the empirical world. They are essences whose very nature is to act, whose power is to “make essential,” to bring into being what they themselves are. Their energeia, their active power, takes concrete form in three further figures whose names come from the Qur'an and the Bible: Joseph (Beauty), Zolaykha (Love), and Jacob (Sorrow). These three figures are, of course, “seen” not as characters in an anecdote about the past but as imagines agentes, active images of the active Imagination.
